lead: Real property a person can own — houses, flats, factory-built and floating homes, land and estates, unusual conversions and burial places — organised by property type, with architectural style and regional house tradition as cross-cutting views; commercial and industrial buildings are out, and garden buildings live in Home Fixtures. Property also holds the materials the home itself is made of: timber and sheet materials, masonry, roofing and insulation, and heritage and reclaimed materials (owner, 2026-11-01).

b.w: Weighed first by every buying guide; a filter and map, never a department.

b.v: freehold > share of freehold > leasehold / condominium > co-operative
b.w: Determines what is actually owned; checked before survey in most jurisdictions.

b.v: roof, walls, damp, plumbing, wiring, heating (RICS Home Survey Levels 1–3)
b.w: Survey follows title.

b.v: EPC A (92+) > B > C > D > E > F > G
b.w: Running cost and comfort; stored only as a view, never for one home.

b.v: bedrooms, layout, outside space, parking
b.w: Last in the order.

depts.t: Dwellings built as houses, whether attached or free-standing, small or grand; one dwelling inside a larger building → Flats & apartments, a house converted from another building → Unusual & converted properties. Architectural style is a period-or-style attribute here; the styles themselves belong to the visual-art taxonomy.
depts.ax: Where does the house stand and how grand is it: in a town row, on a suburban or detached plot, in the countryside, or as a grand seat?
depts.note: Buyer property types first; architectural style and regional tradition are views over the same houses.

b.v: detached > link-detached > semi-detached > end-terrace > mid-terrace
b.w: Listing-portal classification (Rightmove, Zillow).
An attribute and a view (Getty AAT style terms), not a kind.

s.t: Houses built in towns and cities that share walls or sit tightly on a narrow plot; a free-standing house on its own plot → Suburban & detached houses.

k.d: A house sharing one party wall with its neighbour, usually built as a mirror-image pair.

k.a: terrace · row house · row home · brownstone (US) · back-to-back
k.d: A house in a continuous row sharing side walls with neighbours on both sides.
A multi-storey urban house on a small footprint, usually terraced or close-set; historically a grandee's city residence.

x.d: A narrow wood-frame house popularised in New Orleans by 1832, built to meet the same need as north-eastern rowhouses, often several at a time by one builder.

v.d: two shotguns sharing a central wall

x.d: A traditional Japanese wooden townhouse with narrow street frontage stretching deep into the block, earthen walls, tile roof and often small courtyard gardens (tsuboniwa), defining downtown Kyoto for centuries.
A usually old, slim, tall and deep house overlooking a Dutch canal, with a basement, loft and attic once used to store trade goods and a back garden.

v.d: identical or mirrored designs by one builder
built on two plots, e.g. Herengracht

x.d: A Charleston, South Carolina house form with its narrow gable end, two or three bays wide, on the street and a longer side running back from it, found in Federal, Greek Revival and Victorian styles.

k.a: mews property · coach house · carriage house conversion
k.d: A house in a mews: a converted stable or carriage house with living quarters behind large city houses.
A house whose main rooms face an open central yard; the form recurs in China, Morocco, Central Asia and India.
tt: Round or square communal earth building

x.d: One of the two main types of traditional Moroccan house, usually of two or more storeys around an interior symmetrical garden with a central fountain, historically the city home of wealthy merchants and courtiers.
A traditional Chinese house with a courtyard enclosed by buildings on all four sides, prevalent in northern China, notably Beijing and rural Shanxi.

v.d: modern-built courtyard houses in central Beijing

x.d: A large multi-storey building of south-east Fujian for communal living and defence, with load-bearing rammed-earth walls and a wood frame, in which each family holds its own private rooms.
A regional mansion, manor or townhouse of the Indian subcontinent built around a central courtyard (chowk), in brick, sandstone, marble, wood, plaster or granite.

k.d: A terraced building with a shop on the ground floor and living space above, often fronted by arcades or colonnades, typical of Southeast Asia, Sri Lanka and South China.

s.ax: kinds by how the house meets its neighbours: one shared wall, a continuous row, a tall narrow city house, a former mews, a house round a yard

s.t: Houses standing on their own plot, in suburbs and small towns; a house in a row → Town houses, a large country seat → Grand houses.

k.a: single-family detached home · free-standing house · stand-alone house
k.d: A free-standing house sharing no walls with neighbours, on its own plot.

x.d: A traditional Korean house of soil, timber and stone with a tiled (giwa) roof, oiled hanji paper windows and ondol heating, sited on the baesanimsu principle, its form completed in the late Joseon period.
A traditional timber-and-bamboo house of the Malay world, often built without nails from pre-cut jointed parts, with regional roof styles such as Lontik, Lipat Kajang and Limas.
A non-stylistic folk house of L- or T-plan built by tradesmen, associated with New England and the Great Lakes settlers and popular c. 1830–1890 in rural and urban settings.

k.d: A single-storey house, whether detached, semi-detached or terraced, sometimes with rooms set in the roof.

x.d: An earthquake-resistant vernacular house of Assam and Sylhet, a one- or two-storey timber frame on a raised plinth with bamboo or reed wattle-and-daub walls, wraparound verandahs and a high gabled roof, developed after the 1897 earthquake.

k.a: ranch-style house · rambler · rancher · California ranch
k.d: A single-storey American house with a long, low profile and open plan; distinct from a working ranch.
A house whose floors are staggered half a storey apart, common in mid-century US suburbs.
A comfortable detached house with garden, usually in Mediterranean, resort or suburban use.

s.t: Houses in the countryside, from small cottages to working farmhouses and timber holiday homes; a farm with its land → Farm in Land & estates.

k.d: A small, modest house, typically in a rural or semi-rural setting.

x.d: A traditional house of Ireland, the Hebrides and the Scottish Highlands with double dry-stone walls packed with earth, a turf-and-straw thatch on wooden rafters and a central hearth.
An Apulian rural house whose interior is covered by a dry-stone corbelled vault, built of hard limestone or calcareous tufa.
A traditional Sicilian peasant house of local volcanic rock with thick walls and a white roof, found mainly on Pantelleria and Lampedusa, the oldest dating to around the 10th century.

x.a: Cape · Cape Cod cottage · half Cape · three-quarter Cape · full Cape
x.d: A low, broad, one- or one-and-a-half-storey timber-framed house with a steep gabled roof, a large central chimney and a central front door, originating in 17th-century New England.
A Russian second home or summer house on a plot used for growing fruit and vegetables, restricted in Soviet times (1960s–1985 single-storey, unheated, under 25 m²) and unrestricted since 1990.
x.y: 18th century onward; mass building from the 1930s

x.d: A Louisiana and Gulf Coast house thought to derive from French and Spanish colonial forms, with galleries, a broad roof, raised principal rooms and timber frame infilled with brick or bousillage.
A small movable wooden house of Barbados and other West Indian islands, set on blocks or a groundsill and built without nails so it can be dismantled and moved.

k.d: The principal dwelling of a farm, sold with or without its land and outbuildings; see Farm in Land & estates.
tt: Housebarn (house and byre under one roof)
see: a barn turned into a house

x.d: A vernacular medieval timber-framed hall house of south-east England, typically built for a yeoman, with a four-bay plan whose two central bays form a hall open to the roof.

x.a: Fachhallenhaus · Low Saxon house · Niedersachsenhaus · Hallenhaus
x.d: A timber-framed farmhouse of northern Germany and the easternmost Netherlands combining living quarters, byre and barn under one roof around a central threshing floor (Diele).
A byre-dwelling farmhouse found mainly in the central and southern Black Forest of south-west Germany.

v.d: eastern perimeter, the most typical form

x.d: A house type combining log, timber-frame and stone construction in which a wooden support frame round the log living area carries the roof or upper storey.
The rural farmhouse of Catalonia and neighbouring regions, built of rough stone with worked stone at openings in the mountains and of adobe where stone was scarce.
A traditional Japanese vernacular house built of locally abundant materials, in which structure rather than plan is primary; Edo-period farmhouse forms include gasshō-zukuri and honmune-zukuri.
A long single building housing family and livestock; the Dartmoor longhouse is dug into the hillside with rough-stone lower walls and cob above, livestock kept at the lower end.
One of the three basic farmhouse forms of Schleswig-Holstein, found on geest and marshland, whose working area could extend into an L-shape or a four-sided farmstead (Vierseithof).
A variant of the Geestharden farmhouse of the North Frisian islands and Halligen, with red-brick walls, thatched roof, white or blue window frames and a half-open Klöndör door.

A traditional farmhouse type of the Frutigland, Kandertal and Adelboden area of the Bernese Oberland, native since the 15th century, to which two thirds of rural buildings there still conform, often with painted house inscriptions.
A type of longhouse typical of Brittany and Normandy in north-western France.
The most characteristic traditional country house of Cantabria and neighbouring northern Spain, with a sunny south façade and thick rough-masonry walls with ashlar corners.

x.a: New England connected farmstead · big house, little house, back house, barn
x.d: A farmstead in which house, ells, sheds and barns are joined into one continuous building, common in New England and the Canadian Maritimes from the 17th century and also found in England and Wales.

v.n: Delmarva 'big house, little house, colonnade and kitchen'

x.d: A US vernacular house type, two rooms long, one room deep and two full storeys high with side gables and often a rear ell, built from the colonial period in log, frame, brick or stone, chiefly in the Midland.

k.d: A home built within or beside a barn-style shell, with workshop, stable or storage under the same roof.
A house built of stacked logs, from a plain frontier cabin to a modern holiday or kit home.

x.d: A log home in the Finnish tradition, industrialised from 1958 by Honkarakenne in eastern Finland with factory-made prefabricated log components, centred on Karstula.

k.a: Swiss chalet · ski chalet · Alpine house · mountain home
k.d: Wooden Alpine house with heavy, gently sloping roof and wide eaves; now any ski or mountain holiday home.
A house with steep roof planes reaching near the ground, popular for mid-century holiday homes.

x.d: A fortified, usually three-storey residential stone tower built mainly in the Dukagjin region of Kosovo, with a byre on the ground floor, family quarters above and a men's gathering room (oda e burrave).

depts.msum: The ten largest US builders closed a record 44.7 % of new single-family homes in 2024, led by D.R. Horton (NAHB). In the UK, Vistry overtook Barratt as the largest builder in September 2024; Barratt then merged with Redrow in October 2024. 2024 completions: Vistry 17,225, Barratt 14,004 (year to June), Taylor Wimpey 10,593 and Persimmon 10,664; these are counts, not shares, and the reporting years differ.

depts.msum: Completed branded-residence schemes rose from 354 in 2015 to 903 at the end of 2025 (Knight Frank). Hotel brands run about 70 % of operational schemes; Dubai has the most schemes of any city. Savills found a premium of about 35 % over comparable unbranded homes in 2019.

ax: What is the property: a house, a unit in a larger building, a factory-built or floating home, land, a converted or odd building, or a burial space?
key: 1. Is it a house, from cottage to castle, standing alone or in a row? → Houses
2. Is it one dwelling, or a share of one, inside a larger building, or a whole building of flats? → Flats & apartments
3. Was it made in a factory, carried on a chassis, portable, or afloat? → Factory-built, mobile & floating homes
4. Is it land, a farm or estate building, a plot or a parking space? → Land & estates
5. Was the building first made for something other than a house, or built in an odd way (barn, mill, church, fort, folly, cave, tree)? → Unusual & converted properties
6. Is it a lime, earth or distemper finish, a regional period tile, or a salvaged building part? → Heritage & reclaimed materials
7. Is it brick, block, cement, a roof covering, insulation or a flue? → Masonry, roofing & insulation
8. Is it timber, a board, a metal section or a moulding? → Timber & sheet materials
9. Is it a space to bury a body or keep ashes? → Burial places

Precedence: a mobile or floating home is step 3 before step 1; a whole converted building is step 5 but one converted flat is step 2; a farmhouse with its land is step 1, bare farmland step 4; a whole building is steps 1–5, the material it is built from steps 6–8, and a period or reclaimed item (zellige, reclaimed brick, chimney pot) is step 6 before its modern equivalent.
